title: Developing acid-soil-tolerant faba bean varieties to expand faba bean adaption.
description:
Faba bean production in Australia is constrained by soil acidity, particularly in Western Australia, South Australia, southern New South Wales and parts of Victoria, where acidic soils reduce root growth, nodulation, nitrogen fixation, crop vigour and grain yield. Soil acidity also limits the expansion of faba bean into otherwise suitable production environments. While liming remains an important soil management practice, sub-surface acidity is often difficult, slow and costly to remediate, creating a need for complementary genetic solutions that improve crop performance and profitability on affected soils.
Recent GRDC investments have successfully delivered acid-tolerant rhizobia for faba bean, improving nodulation and nitrogen fixation under low pH conditions. However, the effectiveness of these inoculants depends on successful plant-rhizobia interactions, and current elite faba bean germplasm remains poorly adapted to acid soils (pH (CaCl2) <5.0). Developing acid-soil-tolerant varieties is therefore essential to fully realise the benefits of improved rhizobia strains and maximise productivity in acidic soil environments.
This four-year investment will accelerate the development of acid-soil-tolerant faba bean varieties by delivering the germplasm, genetic knowledge and breeding tools required to support long-term genetic improvement. The investment will identify and validate novel sources of acid soil tolerance from Australian and international germplasm, improve understanding of the physiological, biochemical and genetic mechanisms underpinning tolerance, and translate these discoveries into practical breeding outcomes for Australian faba bean breeding programs. Controlled-environment screening, field-based validation and modern genomic approaches will identify and characterise traits associated with improved performance on acidic soils, including traits linked to root growth, nodulation, nitrogen fixation, crop establishment and yield. Activities should address both surface and sub-surface soil acidity and generate robust, field-relevant data to support breeding and selection decisions across target production environments.
A key component of the investment will be the development of validated high-throughput phenotyping methods, screening protocols and molecular markers that enable efficient selection for acid soil tolerance. These tools will support more rapid and cost-effective identification and deployment of favourable alleles within breeding pipelines, accelerating genetic gain for adaptation to acidic soils. Breeder-ready germplasm will incorporate novel acid-soil-tolerance alleles and demonstrating improved performance under acidic soil conditions, with a target yield advantage of at least 10% over benchmark varieties grown on acid soils of pH (CaCl2) below 5.0. Germplasm should be validated across representative production environments and supported by associated genetic, phenotypic and marker datasets to facilitate immediate use in breeding programs.
Strong collaboration with Australian commercial and public faba bean breeding programs will be a core requirement of the investment. Breeding programs should be engaged throughout the project to guide trait prioritisation, validation environments, phenotyping approaches and deployment pathways, ensuring outputs align with breeding priorities and can be rapidly incorporated into breeding pipelines and early-generation selection programs.
The intended outcome is to provide Australian breeders with the genetic resources, screening tools and knowledge required to develop future faba bean varieties with improved adaptation to acid soils, enhanced yield stability and increased productivity. These advances will complement existing soil amelioration practices and acid-tolerant rhizobia, support expansion into suitable regions, improve reliability on acid soils and strengthen the competitiveness and sustainability of the Australian faba bean industry.

title: Enhancing faba bean seed colour and seed size uniformity to increase the value of faba beans and reduce risk of classifi
description:
Faba bean is an important Australian pulse crop and export commodity, supplying premium food and feed markets where visual grain quality is a key determinant of market access, classification and value. Buyers place strong emphasis on seed coat colour, colour retention and seed size uniformity, with these traits directly influencing grading outcomes, market acceptance and the price received throughout the value chain. Variability in visual grain quality, together with seed coat darkening during storage and handling, can increase the risk of downgrades, reduce grower returns and weaken Australia’s competitive advantage in premium export markets.
Although visual grain quality is known to have a strong genetic component, the biological, biochemical and environmental factors influencing seed coat colour stability and seed size uniformity are not well understood. Australian breeding programs currently have limited access to the genetic resources, molecular markers and high-throughput phenotyping tools needed to efficiently improve these traits. Recent advances in genomics, artificial intelligence, digital imaging and data analytics provide new opportunities to accelerate genetic gain and develop more effective breeding solutions.
This four-year investment will develop the knowledge, genetic resources and breeding-enabling tools required to improve seed coat colour stability and seed size uniformity in Australian faba beans. The investment will investigate the genetic, physiological, biochemical and environmental drivers underlying visual grain quality, including the mechanisms responsible for seed coat oxidation and post-harvest darkening. Activities should consider both genetic and non-genetic contributors to trait expression, including the effects of storage conditions, handling practices and environmental influences on grain quality outcomes.
A key component of the investment will be the development and validation of modern phenotyping and analytical tools to enable routine selection for visual grain quality traits. This includes the application of artificial intelligence, machine learning, digital imaging and high-throughput phenotyping approaches to objectively measure seed coat colour stability, seed size uniformity and other commercially important visual attributes. Identification and incorporation of valuable genetic variation for improved seed coat colour stability and seed size uniformity will enable development of breeder-ready germplasm for use in Australian faba bean breeding programs. Germplasm should demonstrate measurable improvements in visual grain quality traits and be supported by associated genetic, phenotypic and validated molecular marker datasets to facilitate rapid integration into breeding pipelines.
Strong and ongoing collaboration with Australian commercial and public faba bean breeding programs will be a core requirement of the investment. Breeding programs should be engaged throughout the project to help guide trait prioritisation, phenotyping methods, validation activities and deployment pathways. This will ensure outputs are aligned with market requirements and breeding priorities and can be rapidly incorporated into crossing blocks, breeding pipelines and early-generation selection programs.
The intended outcome is to provide Australian breeders with the germplasm, molecular markers, phenotyping tools and knowledge required to accelerate the development of future faba bean varieties with improved visual grain quality, greater market suitability and reduced risk of classification downgrades. These advances will help maintain existing market premiums, improve storage and marketing flexibility, protect Australia's reputation as a supplier of high-quality faba beans and strengthen the long-term competitiveness and value of the Australian faba bean industry.

title: Australian Grains Industry Community Trust Collaboration Blueprint.
description:
Description: Trust among rural and urban communities is vital to ensure Australian grain growers are able to conduct business with minimal disruption and continue to innovate and adopt new technologies. In many cases, trust is something that only becomes apparent when it is broken or tested. Measures of trust in the grains industry by the Australian community have changed over time, with a small decrease since 2020.
Decreasing trust can lead to increased regulation, limited market access, disincentives to invest in infrastructure, and reduced industry productivity, profitability and sustainability. Poor levels of trust within an industry make it more likely to be under high levels of scrutiny for practices used on farm, more likely to struggle with talent attraction for future workforce requirements (both on farm and in support and research roles) and reduce the ability for innovation, such as automation, to be adopted as commonplace on farm. There is a high risk that not addressing or maintaining current levels of trust within the grains sector will lead to future challenges impacting grain producers ability to maintain profitability and adopt new technology.
GRDC is seeking a service provider to conduct stakeholder analysis, mapping and consultation to establish clear roles and responsibilities for developing community trust activities in the grains sector. It will bring grains industry stakeholders together, including peak bodies, to develop clear definitions and guidelines for working through issues relating to community trust. The developed blueprint will consequently help guide future activities, including use cases of a data and insights program, a pilot industry communication development program and future education-based activities. Critically, the blueprint requires multi-stakeholder ownership for it to succeed. Getting this right will enable clear GRDC roles and functions that can be used to inform areas of potential investment that can support collaborative industry efforts to build community trust and address industry challenges.
This investment will contribute towards building positive, proactive relationships with the broader community to allow continued innovation, reduce potential innovation bottlenecks and support grain growers with freedom to operate.
Outcome: By December 2027, deliver a community trust collaboration blueprint for the Australian Grains Industry.
Outputs.
Output 1.
Title: Development of a Community Trust Collaboration Blueprint for the Australia Grains Industry.
Description: By December 2027, deliver a community trust collaboration blueprint for the Australian Grains Industry. This will be used to inform GRDC involvement in community trust activities and guide future proposed programs of work. The blueprint will include:
· Establishing the definition of community trust across the sector, and its role in building industry sustainability and specify outcomes.
· Mapping stakeholders, undertaking stakeholder identification and prioritisation and define roles, responsibilities, and best practices for trust building, including open and effective engagement, co-planning strategies and community investment programs.
· Outcomes from a stakeholder workshop to discuss areas for potential collaboration
· Using existing resources, define the quantitative trust baseline, and model and use existing trust drivers to inform objectives for key areas of collaboration.
· Review existing information and consultancies relating to community trust to inform how proposed investment is structured.
In consultation with GRDC a position statement outlining GRDC’s responsibilities and scope aligned to the blueprint will be drafted for GRDC use.

title: Enhancing wheat adaptability for stable yields under variable climates: an integrated genetic and agronomic approach
description: Climate variability is making Australian wheat production more challenging, with drought and interacting stresses such as heat, nutrient limitation and soil constraints increasingly affecting crop performance across regions and seasons. These stresses can reduce yield stability and create greater seasonal risk for growers. One opportunity to address this challenge is to better understand and use wheat’s adaptive plasticity-the ability of wheat plants to adjust growth, development and resource use in response to changing conditions. Adaptive plasticity may help crops reduce yield loss in dry or stressful seasons while maintaining yield potential when conditions are favourable. While wheat breeding programs select for broad adaptation, the specific traits, benchmarks and selection approaches that support adaptive plasticity are not yet routinely defined or targeted. Through this investment, GRDC aims to identify, validate and translate priority plasticity traits into breeder-ready knowledge, datasets, genetic resources and selection guidance. This EOI seeks to identify capable Respondents to participate in a potential multi-stage procurement process to deliver this work.

title: Southern Region pulse research, demonstration, and extension
description: GRDC is investing in a new Southern Region investment to improve the profitability and adoption of pulse crops within farming systems. Pulses are already an important component of these systems, with recent growth driven by lentil production in Victoria and South Australia and expansion into new environments. However, as pulse intensity increases, constraints such as soil acidity and subsoil limitations, herbicide resistance and residue risks, greater disease pressure under tighter pulse sequences, and seasonal variability are becoming more prominent. These challenges, along with emerging opportunities, are identified in GRDC’s pulse crop improvement plans. To address them, the investment will use a regional “hub and spoke” model that combines rigorous field research with practical, paddock-scale learning. Hub sites will target key knowledge gaps, while spoke sites will deliver locally relevant trials, demonstrations, field days and workshops that support growers and advisers and generate high-quality industry datasets. The Regional Pulse Advisory Committee and relevant grower and adviser networks will help set annual priorities for each agroecological zone, supported by expertise from the National Pulse Coordination and Strategy Program in agronomy, crop protection, rhizobia, soils, trial design, data analysis, extension and markets. This approach will retain the flexibility to respond as regional priorities and opportunities evolve.

title: Systematic Reviews to inform the updated NHMRC Statement on Electronic Cigarettes
description:
The Department of Health, Disability and Ageing has provided funding to NHMRC to develop an updated Statement on Electronic Cigarettes (the updated Statement) to replace the 2022 NHMRC CEO Statement on Electronic Cigarettes (the 2022 Statement). The aim of the updated NHMRC Statement is to better understand the current evidence relevant to e-cigarettes and their impacts on individual and population health.
The Electronic Cigarettes Advisory Committee (the Committee), in prioritising topic areas for review in the updated Statement, have advised that two new research questions should be answered by systematic review to inform the updated Statement. These topics are:
Health and wellbeing impacts of electronic cigarettes on young people
Motivators, barriers and enablers for vaping cessation
NHMRC is seeking a Supplier to undertake systematic reviews of the evidence on one or both of the topics to inform the updated Statement.
Potential suppliers may choose to quote to conduct one or both systematic reviews. If a supplier chooses to quote for more than one review, they should address how they intend to deliver all of the services within the required timeframe and any associated cost savings.
Systematic Review 1: Health and wellbeing impacts of electronic cigarettes on young people
The Committee have identified impacts of electronic cigarettes on young people as a priority area for review to inform the updated Statement.
NHMRC is seeking a Supplier to conduct a systematic review assessing global evidence on the health and wellbeing impacts of young people; including the developmental, psychological, emotional and educational, impacts.
See the Statement of Requirement (Attachment C) for further information.
Systematic Review 2: Motivators, barriers and enablers for vaping cessation
The Committee have identified vaping cessation as a priority area for review to inform the updated Statement.
NHMRC is seeking a Supplier to conduct a mixed-methods systematic review assessing global evidence on the motivators, barriers and enablers for vaping cessation. This will include segregated analysis and presentation of qualitative and quantitative data/studies.
See the Statement of Requirement (Attachment C) for further information.
Deliverables for both systematic reviews
Deliverables for each systematic review are:
Deliverable 1: draft research protocol
Deliverable 2: final research protocol
Deliverable 3: preliminary results synthesis and summary of findings table for a single outcome
Deliverable 4: draft systematic review report and draft technical report
Deliverable 5: final systematic review report and final technical report.
Potential suppliers should provide enough detail to ensure NHMRC have a clear understanding of their offer and that all requirements have been addressed. Unclear or contradictory statements may impact upon the assessment of the Response.

DVA serves Australia’s veteran community, through the provision of programmes of care, compensation and commemoration.
DVA’s aim is to secure high quality private hospital care for Entitled Persons delivered for a fair price, at the most convenient locations for Entitled Persons. As the veteran community ages, their capacity to access a wider range of care appropriate to their needs is increasingly important. Managing emerging and different needs of contemporary veterans is also a priority. DVA also aims to continually improve the quality and safety of services, and the health outcomes for DVA clients, through the purchase of evidence-based treatment services.
DVA’s New Approach to Contracting for Private Hospital Services
In the past DVA contracted with Private Hospitals for services to Entitled Persons through a Request for Tenders (RFT).
The current process that DVA is engaging in with Private Hospital providers is not an RFT.
DVA has introduced new arrangements for providers to contract with DVA. This is a simplified contracting model that DVA is using to facilitate engagement with suitably qualified providers.
A summary of the key features of the new arrangements are:
maximising the numbers of participating providers to achieve wide access to private hospitals services for the veteran community;
there is no competition, all qualified providers can participate;
while providers are required to submit the fee tables, there is no requirement for tender submission or evaluation of tenders;
providers self-certify their compliance with DVA’s terms and conditions of the Hospital Services Agreement;
providers can enter into the Hospital Services Agreement at any time and the Hospital Services Agreement will continue until DVA ends the arrangements or the Contracting Entity exits the arrangements with DVA; and
negotiation only on fees to ensure value for money.

title: Western Region pulse research, demonstration, and extension
description: GRDC is proposing a new Western Region investment to help more growers profitably include pulse crops in their farming systems. Pulses such as lupins, lentils, chickpeas and faba beans improve rotations, add nitrogen and support more diverse, profitable systems, yet adoption in Western Australia remains limited by practical barriers around establishment, weed and disease management, harvestability, market access, storage and confidence in local performance. The investment proposes a regional "hub and spoke" model that links practical paddock-scale learning with rigorous field research, with hub sites addressing key knowledge gaps and spoke sites delivering locally relevant trials, demonstrations, field days and workshops that benefit growers and advisers while generating quality datasets for industry. Local grower groups, advisers and stakeholders will shape annual priorities for each agro-ecological zone, drawing on the National Pulse Coordination and Strategy program for expertise in agronomy, crop protection, rhizobia, soils, trial design, data analysis, extension and markets, with flexibility to adjust as opportunities change. By 2032, the investment aims to equip Western Region growers and advisers with the knowledge and confidence to increase pulse production and improve gross margins, strengthening pulse agronomy capability in Western Australia and leaving a better-connected legacy of trial results, resources and practical guidance.

title: Notice of RFT - Refresh and Expansion of the Professions of the Panel of Outreach Program Counsellors for the
description:
This is a pre-release notice to provide advance notification of a proposed RFT for the Refresh and Expansion of the Professions of the Panel.
Please note, eligibility, application requirements, assessment processes, and contractual arrangements will be set out in the forthcoming RFT. No evaluation criteria, scoring methodology, or commercial terms are being released at this stage. The Department reserves the right to modify or cancel the proposed RFT at its discretion.
Background on Open Arms
Open Arms is Australia’s national accredited provider of mental health and wellbeing services for veterans and the families of veterans.
Open Arms provides mental health counselling, relationship counselling, peer support services, and group programs for people with Australian Defence Force (ADF) service (current and former serving members) and their immediate families.
Open Arms provides free and confidential counselling through a national network of multidisciplinary mental health professionals, delivered in dedicated Open Arms centres by the DVA’s staff, or through the Panel; being a network of accredited mental health clinicians, engaged to support the delivery of services on behalf of Open Arms across Australia through the Outreach Program.
Open Arms can provide counselling, care coordination and peer support services to veterans and the families of veterans within an episode of care model, where clients engage with our services for goal directed interventions for a defined period.
Open Arms aims to provide timely access to appropriate services and care, based on a comprehensive holistic assessment and integrated care pathways to meet client needs and support recovery. This includes working in partnership with health systems, including primary health, as well as other community agencies to ensure comprehensive support for our clients.
Background on the Panel and Outreach Program
Open Arms’ Model of Care provides the organisational framework that underpins the delivery of all Outreach Program services. It guides how we support veterans and the families of veterans through trauma-informed, military-aware, recovery-oriented care, while ensuring consistent clinical governance, quality service delivery and positive client outcomes. In 2024 the Panel was established through which Outreach Providers provide Open Arms services to clients. The Panel is the mechanism for Open Arms to engage with Outreach Providers to ensure the highest level of support can be delivered to clients. Only organisations or individuals appointed to the Panel can provide Open Arms Outreach Program Counselling Services.
The categories of services that are delivered through the Panel include:
Outreach Program Counsellors (OPCs), who provide individual, couples, or family counselling
Group Program Facilitators (GPFs), who facilitate evidence-informed, military-aware group programs that strengthen resilience, build practical skills, and promote wellbeing
Clinical Supervisors, who provide professional supervision to Open Arms’ staff.
Outreach Providers on the Panel can provide one, two or all three service streams, depending on their qualifications, experience and the services they are approved to deliver.
Go to the Open Arms website for further information:
https://www.openarms.gov.au/about/open-arms-outreach-program
Expansion of definition of OPC
In 2025 the Veterans’ Entitlements (Treatment Principles) Amendment (Outreach Program Counsellor) Determination 2025 and the Military Rehabilitation and Compensation (Treatment Principles) Amendment (Outreach Program Counsellor) Determination 2025), were enacted which amended the MRCA Treatment Principles (No. MRCC 53/2013) and the Treatment Principles (Instrument 2013 No. R52) – (collectively the Treatment Principles) – to expand the types of professions who can provide Outreach Program Counselling as an Outreach Program Counsellor (OPC). Now that occupational therapists, registered nurses, social workers (general) and counsellors are recognised as additional profession types eligible to apply to become a provider, the Department wishes to update the Panel accordingly through the proposed RFT.
The Department is therefore looking to procure Outreach Providers from the following eligible professions:
a person who is registered with AHPRA as a psychologist;
a person who is registered with AHPRA as an occupational therapist;
a person who is registered with AHPRA as a registered nurse;
a person who is eligible for membership with the Australian Association of Social Workers;
or
a person who is registered:
as a registered clinical counsellor with the Psychotherapy and Counselling Federation of Australia;
as a counsellor at registration category Level 3 or Level 4 with the Australian Counselling Association Limited.
The Department is currently planning to release the RFT to market through publication on AusTender in September 2026, however this timeframe may be subject to change.
Please note that this is not an RFT and does not commit the Department to proceed. The Close Date and Time stated in this notice relates to this pre-release notice only and does not reflect the proposed RFT commencement and closing dates for potential tenderers to lodge their submissions. The RFT, where undertaken, will be published on AusTender and will include the Closing Date and Time for lodgement of submissions.

title: Supply Chain Relationship Data
description:
The Department of Industry, Science and Resources has a requirement for comprehensive company supply chain dataset to support analysis of global supply chains. The data will be integrated into the Department's supply chain mapping platform to help support evidence-based advice to Government.
The data should be sourced primarily from public domain and detail customer–supplier linkages between businesses. The dataset should provide supplier-customer relationship intelligence derived from corporate disclosures, regulatory filings, public statements, annual reports and similar sources, rather than datasets that infer relationships exclusively from trade or logistics activity.
The dataset must have global coverage across industries and regions, reflect current supply chain relationships and be regularly maintained.
In addition to the company supply chain dataset, the following capabilities will be viewed favourably but are not mandatory:
· A comprehensive business facilities dataset containing business location information, including:
o Physical addresses
o Latitude and longitude coordinates
o Facility type classifications, including but not limited to offices, warehouses, distribution centres and manufacturing facilities
Delivery Requirements

publicQuestions.question:
Hi,

We have four questions below regarding the tender documents and would appreciate clarification from the EGC team. Thank you.

1. PART D1 Pricing Schedule

The schedule includes individual sensor part numbers with NO reference to what Indicator they are used with. It also separately lists YSI Pro Quotro Maultiparameter Meters or Hach HQ Portable Multiparameter Meters. Can you please confirm if these are used together or do the Multiparameter meters have their own sensors. If the Multiparameter meters do have their own sensor please provide details of parameter for each individual meter.

2. For the consumable costs we will allow for reagents and reference kits required to test. In addition to this do you want us to replace DO sensor caps every calibration or AS REQUIRED (at additional cost)?

3. Can you confirm if pH/Fluoride/conductivity/DO sensors fail during calibration that EGW will procure and supply replacements which will then be re-calibrated at addition cost (refer schedule of rates pricing) at an agreed time in the future or at the next scheduled calibration visit.

4. Our intention is to base pricing on completing all sites over an 8 day period with a set itinery to provide the most cost effective offer. Is this Ok or do you want pricing based on a separate visit to each individual site?
publicQuestions.answer:
Hi Aimee,

Please refer the below answer:

1. PART D1 Pricing Schedule

The schedule includes individual sensor part numbers with NO reference to what Indicator they are used with. It also separately lists YSI Pro Quotro Maultiparameter Meters or Hach HQ Portable Multiparameter Meters. Can you please confirm if these are used together or do the Multiparameter meters have their own sensors. If the Multiparameter meters do have their own sensor please provide details of parameter for each individual meter.

ANSWER: The YSI Pro Quattro and Hach HQ meters are separate meter types. The sensors listed in the schedule are associated with the relevant meters.

2. For the consumable costs we will allow for reagents and reference kits required to test. In addition to this do you want us to replace DO sensor caps every calibration or AS REQUIRED (at additional cost)?

ANSWER: DO Sensor caps are to be replaced as required only.

3. Can you confirm if pH/Fluoride/conductivity/DO sensors fail during calibration that EGW will procure and supply replacements which will then be re-calibrated at addition cost (refer schedule of rates pricing) at an agreed time in the future or at the next scheduled calibration visit.

ANSWER: Ideally, you can provide a price to provide a replacement part at a minimum. There will then be decisions made with regards to who installs and completes basic calibration

4. Our intention is to base pricing on completing all sites over an 8 day period with a set itinerary to provide the most cost-effective offer. Is this Ok or do you want pricing based on a separate visit to each individual site?

ANSWER: Yes, EGW is happy for pricing to be based on completing all sites over such a schedule subject to agreed itinerary and site access.

title: Call for Expressions of Interest: System Restart Service (SWIS-wide)
description:
AEMO is seeking Expressions of Interest (EOI) to understand the availability, location and readiness of Facilities that may be able to provide System Restart Service across the SWIS.

Previous System Restart Service engagements have indicated that other existing or new Facilities may also be capable of providing System Restart Service, subject to necessary site works, testing and lead times.

AEMO invites Market Participants, or prospective Market Participants, with Facilities capable of providing System Restart Service to make submissions for:

* a Facility with System Restart Service capability to commence from 23 October 2028 (EOI Part 1); and

* a Facility with System Restart Service capability to commence only after October 2030 (EOI Part 2).

AEMO welcomes submissions for either existing or proposed Facilities with different technology configurations to submit an EOI. The EOI will be used by AEMO to determine the requirements of a subsequent tender, such as the location of the service (Sub-Network) and service commencement period.

AEMO will specifically use the information from the EOI to:

* identify a short-list of candidates that are able to meet the System Restart Standard;

* assess the efficacy to provide System Restart Services;

* review and potentially amend the System Restart Standard, including the Electrical Sub-Network boundaries (i.e. this is to determine the location AEMO will be tendering for the System Restart Service); and

* confirm with short-listed candidates any necessary upgrades or capital works to be compliant with the future System Restart Standard and the System Restart Service Specification and identify associated timelines to provide the service.

All submissions:

* must be provided in good faith but are not binding on the respondent; and

* will be treated as confidential information under applicable Electricity System and Market Rules.

Submissions must be provided via VendorPanel in accordance with the EOI Guideline by 5pm AWST on 9 November 2026.

title: Ecotourism Opportunities in Queensland
description: This project seeks to identify and prioritise ecotourism opportunities in Queensland that are globally competitive, aligned with visitor demand, and capable of delivering strong conservation outcomes. It will provide the government and tourism industry with a set of clear and evidence-based recommendations on where Queensland is best positioned to compete and succeed in ecotourism, and which opportunities should be prioritised to maximise economic, environmental and visitor outcomes.

vendorPanelDetails.buyerAddress:
515 St Pauls Terrace
Fortitude Valley, Queensland 4006
Australia
vendorPanelDetails.buyerDescription: As the peak destination marketing organisation, Tourism and Events Queensland leads marketing campaigns which showcase Queensland's breathtaking natural wonders, vibrant cities, and unique cultural experiences. Through strategic partnerships with industry stakeholders and regional tourism organizations, we foster a thriving tourism ecosystem that generates economic growth and creates jobs across the state.
vendorPanelDetails.queryCutoffAtRaw: Friday 25 September 2026 05:00 PM (E. Australia Standard Time)
vendorPanelDetails.desiredOutcomes: The successful Respondent will deliver an independent, evidence-based research and analysis that identifies and prioritises new ecotourism opportunities in Queensland. The work must provide a clear, defensible and market-informed assessment of where Queensland is best positioned to compete and succeed in ecotourism, and the opportunities that should be prioritised to maximise economic, environmental and visitor outcomes.
buyerQuestions: What are visitors seeking from ecotourism experiences, and which source markets and visitor segments offer the greatest potential for Queensland’s ecotourism sector?
What are the leading global ecotourism case studies, and what insights from a comparative analysis of their development models can be applied to Queensland?
What new ecotourism opportunities offer the greatest potential for Queensland to capitalise on its natural assets and cultural strengths while meeting future visitor demand?
Which ecotourism opportunities should Queensland prioritise to maximise visitor, economic and conservation outcomes, and what factors should inform their prioritisation?
What tenure, Native Title, approval, governance and facilitation pathways are required to progress each priority ecotourism opportunity?

The Queensland Government Supplier Code of Conduct sets out the expectations that government has of businesses that want to sell their goods or services to the government, and outlines what constitutes a responsible supplier.
Compliance with the Queensland Government Supplier Code of Conduct is a mandatory requirement of this ITO Process.
Your organisation warrants adherence to the Queensland Government Supplier Code of Conduct.

For the next 6 questions, Suppliers are required to demonstrate that they have the financial capability to provide all the requirements over the term of the Contract. Short-listed Suppliers may be asked to provide further financial information if required. Are there any significant events, matters or circumstances which have arisen within the past 12 months that could significantly affect the operations of the Supplier? If yes, please give details.

Are there, or have there been any:

a). Bankruptcy and/or de-registration actions; or

b). Insolvency proceedings (including voluntary administration, application to wind up, or other similar action)

either actual or threatened, against the Supplier in the past three years? If so, what (if any) remedial action has been taken?
If yes, please supply details.

Are there any other factors that could adversely impact the financial ability of the Supplier to successfully perform the obligations contemplated by this ITO?
If yes, please supply details.

Does the Supplier acknowledge that, if they are shortlisted, they may be required to provide further financial information (including audited financial statements for the past three years) to verify the Suppliers financial capacity?

Provide details of any actual, potential or perceived Conflict of Interest that exists or may arise in relation to the Invitation Process or performance of the Contract (including any conflict of interest with department staff or other suppliers).

If there is nothing to declare, insert “Nil”.

Is the Supplier a small to medium enterprise?

Small – a business employing less than 20 people.

Medium – a business employing 20 or more people, but less than 200 people.

Note: people are both employees and contractors employed by the Supplier.

Provide a brief description of the business and its overall qualifications to meet the requirements. Background information may include the number of years of relevant experience, rate of growth, size, locations, annual turnover etc.

Provide details of 2 other government customers to which the Supplier has provided Services under the Contract.

title: ITSM Platform Review
description:
The University of Southern Queensland (UniSQ) is seeking responses for the provision and implementation of a modern Information Technology Service Management (ITSM) platform to support reliable, secure, scalable, and efficient service management across the University.

The scope of this procurement includes the supply of the ITSM platform, implementation services, configuration, data migration, system integration, user training, ongoing support, and managed service requirements. The proposed solution must align with industry best practice service management frameworks, including ITIL, and support UniSQ's operational and strategic objectives.

UniSQ's objective is to establish an ITSM solution that is cyber security and privacy compliant, integration-ready, and capable of enhancing service reliability, user experience, workflow automation, reporting and analytics, knowledge management, governance, and continual service improvement. The solution should also support UniSQ's broader digital transformation roadmap and future service delivery requirements.

publicQuestions.question:
ServiceNow is supporting enquiries from our partner network for this tender. It sounds like University of Southern Queensland (USQ) is seeking a single vendor approach to this, with provision of the platform, implementation services, and support services delivered by a single vendor. ServiceNow works with 30+ universities across Australia, and all universities procure their licenses for the SeviceNow ITSM platform directly from ServiceNow, and contract with their implementation and partners separately. This provided the most flexibility to the universities, as they can choose the partner/s best able to deliver each specific service or project outcome. A direct relationship with ServiceNow also opens up preferential commercial options for universities, with a CAUDIT-aligned master ordering agreement and EFTSL-based price book that is beneficial for universities.

Is USQ open to a similar arrangement of a direct platform relationship with ServiceNow?

As the leading ITSM platform in the market, we will happily support USQ and our partners in the market, with whatever option best supports USQ's needs.

publicQuestions.question:
Hi

ID	Part B Ref	Requirement / Context	Question to UniSQ	Priority

1. CURRENT PLATFORM, CUSTOMISATION AND DATA MIGRATION

1	8.1	Addendum 1: data migration "should be addressed through the respondent's proposed implementation methodology".	Is the current ITSM platform deployed on-premises or as a hosted/SaaS service, and does it integrate to on-premises systems that would require network connectivity or a secure gateway from the new platform? 3	8.1	Section 8.1 requires an implementation approach and timeline.	For data migration, could you please indicate the approximate volume and retention expectation for: open tickets, closed ticket history and the number of years to be retained, attachments, knowledge articles, CMDB records, and service catalogue and workflow configuration?	P1

4	8.1	Addendum 3 Q4 confirms phased delivery approaches may be proposed.	Is full historical data migration required at go-live, or is a phased approach acceptable where in-flight and recent records migrate before cutover and the historical archive follows in a second pass?	P1

2. IDENTITY AND ACCESS

5	7.1	Section 7.1 requires enterprise identity and access management integration.	Which identity provider is used for staff, and is the same directory used for students, or are staff and student identities held in separate directories? Which SSO protocol is required (SAML 2.0 or OIDC), and is SCIM provisioning required in addition to single sign-on?	P1

6	7.1 / 6.5	Section 6.5 requires configurable approval workflows.	Where user attributes such as department, cost centre, manager, campus and location are used for approval routing and entitlement, which system is the authoritative source for those attributes?	P1

7	7.1	Section 7.1 covers identity and access management.	Beyond permanent staff, which populations must be supported for access and request fulfilment, for example casual and sessional academics, contractors, honorary and adjunct appointments, research partners, and alumni? Is student identity provisioning driven by the enrolment or student management system?	P2

3. INTEGRATION LANDSCAPE

8	5.4 / 6.8	ITO scope refers to integration with "IAM, ERP and monitoring tools". Addendum 1: "Respondents should outline their recommended technology architecture and integration approach."	Could you please provide the list of systems that must integrate with the ITSM platform, indicating which are mission-critical for go-live and which are desirable in a later phase?	P1

9	6.8	Section 6.8 covers out-of-the-box integrations and integration architecture.	For each system in scope, is the requirement read-only visibility (status, notifications, approvals), or full read-write action execution (submitting requests, triggering provisioning, updating records)?	P1

10	6.8	Section 6.8 covers integration architecture.	Does UniSQ operate an integration platform, middleware or API gateway (for example Boomi, MuleSoft or Azure API Management) that third-party platforms are expected to route through, or are direct API and webhook integrations acceptable? Are there restrictions on direct system-to-system calls?	P1

11	5.4	Section 5.4 requires enterprise platform integration.	For the ERP and finance systems, what are the intended use cases for integration, for example asset procurement and receipting, cost centre validation for approvals, or chargeback and internal recovery of IT costs?	P2

12	5.4 / 6.6	Section 6.6 (Mandatory) requires request fulfilment workflow.	Which HR or payroll system triggers joiner, mover and leaver events, and is onboarding and offboarding orchestration in scope for the initial deployment? Does offboarding orchestration extend to student accounts at completion or withdrawal?	P1

13	5.4	Section 5.4 requires enterprise platform integration.	Is the student management system in scope for integration, and if so which service scenarios are expected, for example student IT account issues, enrolment-driven access provisioning, or lab and software entitlement?	P2

14	5.2 / 6.8	Section 5.2 requires a self-service portal as a single entry point.	Is the learning management system in scope for service desk support and integration, and should teaching-related incidents be raised, triaged and reported within the ITSM platform?	P2

15	5.2 / 7.5	Section 7.5 covers ongoing technical service delivery.	Is telephony or contact centre integration required for the service desk (for example screen pop, click to dial, call logging), and which telephony platform is in use? How many shared or functional mailboxes require email-to-ticket intake?	P2

4. CMDB, ASSET MANAGEMENT AND DISCOVERY

16	6.3	Addendum 3 Q1 confirms Ivanti Endpoint Manager and software asset management are in the current environment. Addendum 3 Q2 confirms native or integrated third-party discovery is acceptable.	Should the proposed platform ingest asset and configuration data from Ivanti Endpoint Manager and the existing software asset management capability, or is the expectation that the ITSM platform assumes responsibility for discovery? If the Ivanti tooling is being retained, please confirm the intended period of coexistence.	P1

17	6.3	Section 6.3 covers CMDB and asset management.	Which endpoint and mobile device management tools are deployed across the estate (for example Microsoft Intune, Jamf or equivalent) for Windows, macOS, iOS and Android, and should the ITSM platform ingest compliance and configuration data from each?	P1

18	6.3	Section 6.3 requires CMDB capability.	What level of CMDB capability is required: asset and configuration inventory with ownership and lifecycle, or full dependency and service mapping supporting impact analysis for incident and change? Which CI classes are in scope (end user devices, servers, network, applications, business services, cloud resources)?	P1

19	6.3	Section 6.3 covers asset management scope.	Which asset categories fall within scope beyond standard end user computing, for example teaching and computer lab fleets, audio visual and classroom technology, research computing and instrumentation, and library or loan equipment? Are student-owned devices in scope for support or asset records?	P2

20	6.3	Section 6.3 covers asset lifecycle.	Is the ITSM platform expected to act as the system of record for asset financials such as purchase value, depreciation and warranty, or should it ingest that data from the finance or procurement system?	P2

5. SERVICE CATALOGUE, WORKFLOW AND AUTOMATION

21	6.4	Section 6.4 requires a service catalogue structure.	Approximately how many service catalogue items and request types are in scope for initial delivery, and how many distinct fulfilment teams or resolver groups will they route to?	P1

22	6.5	Section 6.5 requires configurable workflows and catalogue governance.	How many active workflows and automations exist today, and what is the expected approval complexity: single-level or multi-level, sequential or parallel, and are approvals typically role-based, cost-centre-based or delegation-based?	P1

23	6.5	Section 6.5 covers configurable workflows.	Is Microsoft Power Automate or another orchestration tool currently used to drive approvals or automation? Should the new platform trigger those existing flows, or handle orchestration natively and replace them?	P1

24	6.6	Section 6.6 Request Fulfilment Workflow is a mandatory requirement.	Which request types does UniSQ most want automated end to end at go-live, for example account and access provisioning, software entitlement, hardware requests, or shared mailbox and distribution list changes?	P1

6. PROCESS DESIGN

25	6.2	Section 6.2 requires core ITSM process management including change enablement. Are change freeze or blackout periods aligned to semester and examination cycles?	P2

26	6.2	Section 6.2 requires core ITSM process management including major incident handling.	What is the current major incident process, which channels are used for war room collaboration and stakeholder communication (for example Microsoft Teams), and is mass notification to affected staff and students required from the platform?	P2

27	6.2	Section 6.2 requires service level management.	Could you please confirm the SLA and priority matrix in use, the business hours calendars that apply including any variation across campuses, semester periods and examination windows, and the escalation rules expected at go-live?	P2

7. CHANNELS, EXPERIENCE AND REPORTING

P2

8. ENVIRONMENTS AND SERVICE CONTINUITY

31	7.4	Section 7.4 covers environment management.	How many non-production environments are required (development, test, user acceptance, training), and is a separate training environment with representative data expected?	P2

Does UniSQ have specific recovery time and recovery point objectives that the platform must meet, and are there defined availability or maintenance window requirements, including periods such as enrolment and examinations where change must be restricted?	P2

9. COMMERCIAL AND CONTRACT

33	8.6	The pack includes both QITC Schedule 1 (Price and Payment Terms) and QITC Schedule 2 (Project Implementation and Payment Plan). Schedule 1 states it is not required where Schedule 2 applies.	Could you please confirm which schedule is the authoritative pricing vehicle, and whether UniSQ will issue a pricing template? As these volumes are not disclosed, could UniSQ confirm the total staff population expected to have access to the platform, and whether students are included in that population for licensing purposes? Where respondents price against stated assumptions, can pricing be reconciled at contract formation if actual volumes differ materially?	P1

Could you please clarify whether the ongoing support requirement covers platform support and administration only, or a managed service desk including L1 staffing? If L1 is in scope, what coverage hours, channels and volumes should respondents price against?	P1

publicQuestions.question:
We have the following queries which would appreciate Council's response:

1) ISO 9001 requirement

The Services state that all services, including subconsultant services, are to be carried out under a QMS certified to AS/NZS ISO 9001, except where the Principal accepts otherwise, whereas the Tender Schedule asks whether the Tenderer has either an ISO 9001-certified system or can demonstrate equivalent systems are in place.

Please confirm that a consultant without third-party ISO 9001 certification may submit a conforming tender where it demonstrates an equivalent documented QMS, project-specific Quality Plan, independent checking and QA records acceptable to Council.

2) Construction budget definition

The Services identify an early construction estimate of approximately $2 million, but state that an indicative construction budget has not yet been determined.

Please confirm whether $2 million is to be treated as a design budget/target, and whether it includes or excludes contamination remediation, Foreshore Road/deceleration lane works, TfNSW works, landscape works, lighting/CCTV, authority charges, preliminaries, contingency and GST.

3) Overall completion milestone

Council anticipates award in late November 2026 and commencement in mid-December 2026. The specified programme includes 12 weeks for concept review/endorsement, 12 weeks for community consultation, two-week reviews at both 50% and 75% detailed design, followed by IFT and IFC.

Please confirm Council's required target dates for endorsed Concept Design, 50% DD, 75% DD, IFT and IFC, and whether the 12-week concept approval and 12-week community consultation periods may overlap.

4) Existing survey information

The Scope refers to available survey, utilities, easements and levels, while the pricing schedule separately nominates a registered surveyor for boundary definition.

Please confirm exactly what existing feature/topographic, cadastral/boundary, easement and level survey information Council will provide, including its format and currency. Is a new registered cadastral/boundary survey required within the base scope?

5) Geotechnical and pavement investigations

Existing 2018 TfNSW investigations include test pits to approximately 1.8–1.9 m depth, with basecourse and underlying marine sand deposits recorded.

Please confirm whether Council considers the existing TfNSW geotechnical information sufficient for detailed pavement design, or whether the Consultant is expected to allow for new geotechnical investigation, pavement cores/test pits, DCP/CBR testing and laboratory testing in the base tender price.

6) Supplementary contamination investigations

The Scope requires the Consultant to identify and undertake additional investigations as necessary, including supplementary contamination investigations, subject to Council approval.

Should the tender lump sum include an allowance for supplementary contamination sampling/testing, or should such investigation be treated as an additional service/provisional allowance once the PSI, DSI and RAP have been reviewed and specific data gaps identified?

7) Environmental/remediation consultant scope

The existing site investigations identify asbestos-containing material and uncontrolled/fill-related contamination constraints.

Please confirm whether the Environmental Consultant's role is limited to interpreting and incorporating the existing PSI/DSI/RAP into the design, or whether the commission is also to include preparation/revision of the RAP, remedial works specifications, asbestos management documentation, validation planning/reporting and post-remediation site validation.

8) NSW EPA Site Auditor

Please confirm whether an EPA-accredited Site Auditor is required for this project or for Council's Part 5 determination. If required, is the Auditor to be engaged and paid directly by Council, or included within the Lead Consultant's lump sum?

9) Flooding and overland-flow assessment

The additional investigation scope lists a flooding and overland-flow assessment but does not define the modelling level required.

Please confirm whether this requires a project-specific hydraulic/flood model and formal 1% AEP assessment, or whether review of Council's existing flood information together with site grading, stormwater and overland-flow assessment is sufficient. Please also confirm whether existing Council flood models and GIS/model files will be supplied.

10) Sydney Water triple stormwater pipeline information

Council advises that scanning of the triple Sydney Water stormwater pipeline is currently being undertaken and will be provided.

Please confirm when the scan results will be available, the survey/utility quality level to be provided, and whether the information will include surveyed horizontal and vertical positions suitable for detailed design.

11) Sydney Water WSC / Building Plan Approval

The Scope notes that investigations may trigger the need for a Water Servicing Coordinator and formal Sydney Water Building Plan Approval.

Should the tender include engagement of a Water Servicing Coordinator and preparation/management of the Building Plan Approval application, or should this be treated as a separately authorised service if the pipeline investigation confirms it is required?

12) Authority application and statutory fees

Please confirm that Sydney Water, TfNSW, Ausgrid, Sydney Airport and other statutory application, plan-checking, inspection, bond, WAD, ROL, utility connection and authority fees will be paid directly by Council and are not to be included in the Consultant's lump-sum professional fee.

13) TfNSW WAD scope

TfNSW has already indicated concurrence in principle to the access locations/deceleration lane subject to detailed design approval and requires a Works Authorisation Deed, plan-checking fees and potentially a performance bond.

Please confirm whether the Lead Consultant is required to manage the full TfNSW WAD process through approval, including preparation of all TfNSW road design documentation, responses to comments and coordination of the WAD, or only provide the technical design package for Council to administer the WAD.

14) Extent of Foreshore Road works

TfNSW requires left-in/left-out movements, a deceleration lane, crossings and associated road/drainage works to TfNSW requirements.

Please confirm that the Foreshore Road deceleration lane, road widening/kerb works, drainage modifications, signage/linemarking and vehicular crossings form part of the detailed design, IFT and IFC scope.

15) Traffic survey requirements

The Scope lists traffic and parking surveys as potential additional investigations.

Does Council hold recent classified traffic counts, turning movement data, parking demand information or pump-track patronage forecasts? If not, please confirm the type, duration and locations of traffic surveys expected to be included in the tender price.

16) Council-appointed Quantity Surveyor

The Services state that Council will engage a third-party QS for the three concept estimates, 50%, 75% and IFT estimates and the IFT BOQ.

Please confirm that no QS fee is required within the Consultant's lump sum and that the Lead Consultant's obligation is limited to supplying coordinated design information, responding to QS queries and participating in value-management/cost-review activities.

17) Construction “site management plans”

The Services list “site management plans for construction” among the required standard documents.

Please clarify which specific construction site-management plans are to be prepared by the design consultant. We assume contractor SWMS, detailed Construction Environmental Management Plan, Construction Traffic Management Plan, site establishment plan and construction methodology remain the future Contractor's responsibility unless specifically identified otherwise.

18) IFT tender/procurement assistance

The documents are to be used to call construction tenders, after which the Consultant will complete remaining documentation and progress to IFC.

Please confirm whether the consultancy scope includes assistance during the construction tender period, such as responding to tender RFIs, preparing addenda, technical tender evaluations or tender interviews. If so, please nominate the expected tender duration and allowance for RFIs/addenda.

19) IFC trigger and contractor-driven amendments

Please confirm whether IFC is expected to comprise incorporation of Council's final IFT comments and agreed tender clarifications only, or whether redesign arising from the successful contractor's alternative materials, methodologies or value-engineering proposals is also to be included within the lump sum.

20) Additional investigation approval and commercial treatment

Council requires any additional investigations to receive approval before commencement.

Please confirm that investigations identified after review of the existing information but not capable of being reasonably defined at tender stage may be submitted to Council for approval and treated as an additional/provisional service rather than being deemed included in the fixed lump sum.
publicQuestions.answer:
1) Council confirms that a consultant without third-party AS/NZS ISO 9001 certification may submit a conforming tender, provided it can demonstrate an equivalent documented Quality Management System (QMS) acceptable to Council.

Tenderers should provide details of their quality management procedures, including quality assurance processes, document control, independent review/checking procedures and project-specific quality management measures, for Council's assessment.

2) The $2 million construction budget is indicative only and is provided for tendering purposes. The final project budget will be refined as the design develops. For the purposes of preparing fee proposals, the indicative construction budget should be assumed to include all project delivery costs associated with the proposed works, including contamination remediation, Foreshore Road and deceleration lane works, TfNSW-related works, landscape works, lighting and CCTV, authority and approval charges, contractor preliminaries, contingencies and GST. Tenderers should use these assumptions when preparing their submissions.

3) There are no prescribed target dates for individual design milestones. Tenderers are to develop and submit their own programme for delivery of the Services based on the project requirements.

The Consultant is to allow adequate time within its programme for Council review and approval at each stage of the design process. At the submission of the draft Concept Design package, the Consultant is to allow up to twelve (12) weeks for Council review, consideration and endorsement prior to finalisation of the Concept Design. Similarly, at the submission of draft Detailed Design, IFT and IFC packages, the Consultant is to allow up to two (2) weeks for Council review before receiving approval to proceed to the next design milestone.

The twelve (12) week community consultation period may overlap with Council's review period where appropriate. The anticipated process is that the Consultant will prepare a Draft Concept Design incorporating viable options for Council consideration. Council will review and endorse a preferred option, following which a single concept option will be developed for community consultation. Community consultation is anticipated to occur over a period of up to twelve (12) weeks. Feedback received during consultation is to be considered and, where appropriate, incorporated into either the final Concept Design or the subsequent Detailed Design phase, depending on project timing and staging.

The Consultant's final design milestone is the submission of IFC documentation following appointment of the construction contractor and completion of the required IFC review process.

4) The information made available by Council is limited to the documentation included within the Tender Appendix. Tenderers should base their submissions on the information provided and satisfy themselves as to its suitability for the proposed Services.

Where additional survey information is required to complete the design, including feature and level survey, utility investigation, easement verification, cadastral definition or boundary survey, such services are to be included within the Consultant's base scope. Available survey information will generally be provided in PDF and DWG format where available.

Tenderers should assume that any additional survey necessary to support design development, approvals and construction documentation is their responsibility and should be allowed for within their fee proposal.

5) The Tender Appendix includes the existing TfNSW geotechnical information together with Council's more recent site investigation documentation and Remedial Action Plan (B1, B2 and B3). Tenderers are required to review and consider all available information provided as part of the tender documentation.

Council considers the available information to be suitable for concept and preliminary design purposes; however, it should not be relied upon as being sufficient to support detailed pavement design and final construction documentation.

Accordingly, Tenderers shall allow within their base scope for any geotechnical investigations considered necessary to develop and verify the detailed pavement design and complete a final constructable design. This may include, where required, additional test pits, pavement investigations, DCP and/or CBR testing, laboratory testing and associated geotechnical assessment.

6) Tenderers shall allow for supplementary contamination sampling and testing where, following review of the available PSI, DSI and RAP documentation, specific data gaps are identified that are necessary to complete the design and support delivery of a constructable project.

Any investigations that can be reasonably anticipated as being necessary to develop the design, confirm remediation requirements, or support project delivery are to be included within the Consultant's base fee.

Where a service or investigation cannot be reasonably defined at tender stage and its requirement is dependent on findings arising later during project delivery, the Consultant should clearly identify the potential scope within its methodology and provide an indicative provisional allowance. Any such investigations will be subject to Council approval prior to commencement.

7) The Environmental Consultant's role is intended to be limited to interpretation of the existing environmental investigations (including the PSI/DSI and RAP) and incorporation of the identified contamination, asbestos and remediation constraints into the design. Tenderers are to review and rely upon the existing PSI/DSI and RAP documentation provided and allow for the environmental input necessary to inform and support the design.

The scope does not include preparation or revision of the RAP, asbestos management documentation, validation planning or reporting, environmental supervision of remediation works, post-remediation site validation, preparation of remediation completion reports or environmental sign-off.

Notwithstanding the above, where remediation-related requirements affect the design, tender documentation or constructability of the project, the Consultant shall incorporate the requirements of the existing RAP and environmental investigations into the design documentation as appropriate.

Any remediation, asbestos management, validation and associated compliance activities will be undertaken separately.

8) Council does not currently require the engagement of an EPA-accredited Site Auditor as part of this design commission or for the purposes of the Part 5 assessment.

Tenderers are not required to include for the engagement of an EPA-accredited Site Auditor within their fee proposal. Should Council determine that a Site Auditor is required at a later stage due to project approvals, remediation requirements, regulatory advice or other project-specific considerations, the Site Auditor will be engaged separately by Council.

9) The flooding and overland flow assessment is to assess existing flooding and drainage constraints affecting the site and demonstrate that the proposed development will maintain or improve the existing flood and overland flow behaviour of the site and surrounding land.

Council has provided available flood mapping information within the Tender Appendix. Council does not currently have a hydraulic flood model available for tenderers.

Tenderers are to review the available flood information, assess existing and proposed site levels, stormwater drainage design and overland flow paths, and demonstrate that the proposed works will not adversely impact flood behaviour, flood storage, overland flow paths, stormwater drainage performance or adjoining properties.

Tenderers are responsible for determining the level of assessment necessary to support their design. Where the Consultant considers additional hydraulic analysis or flood modelling is necessary to demonstrate compliance with the above requirements, the proposed methodology, assumptions and associated cost allowances should be identified within their submission.

Tenderers should assume that any investigations, analysis or modelling reasonably required to support a constructable design and demonstrate no worsening of flood impacts are included within the base scope of services.

10) Scanning of the Sydney Water triple stormwater pipeline is currently being undertaken by Council. The resulting information will be provided to the successful Consultant at project commencement.

The information will be derived from CCTV inspection and sonde tracing and is expected to include surveyed horizontal and vertical positions of the pipeline suitable for design development. However, Council cannot currently confirm the survey quality level, accuracy or utility quality level classification that will be assigned to the information and tenderers should assume it will be provided in the form received by Council.

The Consultant is responsible for reviewing the information provided and determining whether any supplementary survey, utility investigation, potholing or verification is required to support detailed design, approvals and construction documentation.

Any additional investigations reasonably required to complete a constructable design should be included within the Consultant's base scope.

11) Council understands that the proposed works may interact with existing Sydney Water assets and that approvals may be required from Sydney Water depending on the final design and the outcomes of utility investigations.

Tenderers are to allow for investigation of Sydney Water asset constraints and identification of all relevant approval requirements associated with the proposed works.

At this stage, Council has not confirmed the final approval pathway, including whether a Water Servicing Coordinator (WSC), Building Plan Approval (BPA), Section 73 requirements or other Sydney Water approvals will be required.

Council currently anticipates that a Water Servicing Coordinator will likely be required in relation to the proposed slip lane works over the Sydney Water stormwater main. Additional Sydney Water approvals may also be required if the proposed design includes connection of new stormwater infrastructure to a Sydney Water asset.

Tenderers are to clearly identify any assumptions regarding Sydney Water approvals in their submission and nominate any exclusions from their lump sum fee. Any services excluded from the lump sum should be separately identified with an indicative provisional cost.

12) Authority and statutory application fees are to be paid directly by Council and are not to be included within the Consultant's lump-sum fee.

Where authority applications, approvals, plan checking, inspections, permits, bonds, utility connection charges or other statutory fees are required by Sydney Water, TfNSW, Ausgrid, Sydney Airport or other authorities, the relevant invoice or fee notice is to be provided to Council for direct payment.

The Consultant shall, however, allow for the preparation, coordination and submission of applications and supporting technical documentation required as part of the Services, unless specifically excluded within their proposal.

13) The Consultant is to allow for management of the full TfNSW approval process associated with the proposed works, including coordination of the Works Authorisation Deed (WAD) process, preparation of all required TfNSW road design documentation, responses to TfNSW comments and requests for information, and progression of submissions through to approval.

The Consultant shall act as the primary technical interface with TfNSW throughout the design and approval process and shall incorporate all reasonable TfNSW requirements into the design documentation.

Council may assist with administration and stakeholder liaison activities where required; however, Tenderers should assume responsibility for managing and obtaining the necessary TfNSW technical approvals as part of their base scope.

14) Council confirms that the Foreshore Road works, including the deceleration/slip lane, road widening, kerb and gutter works, drainage modifications, signage, line marking, vehicular access arrangements and all associated civil works required to satisfy TfNSW requirements, form part of the Detailed Design, IFT and IFC scope.

Tenderers are to allow for the preparation, coordination and approval of all road design documentation required by TfNSW and to manage the associated approval process. It is anticipated that the Foreshore Road works will be subject to a separate review and approval process by TfNSW in addition to Council's design review process.

Tenderers should demonstrate previous experience in the design and approval of works within the TfNSW road corridor, including obtaining TfNSW approvals and managing review timeframes associated with external agency approvals.

Tenderers should also recognise that TfNSW approval timeframes may differ from the overall project programme and should plan accordingly. Consultants are expected to demonstrate an understanding of potential project staging and delivery approaches, including scenarios where the car park works may proceed independently while TfNSW review and approval of the Foreshore Road works remains ongoing.

15) Council has not provided traffic count data, turning movement counts, parking demand assessments or patronage forecasts as part of the Tender Appendix.

Tenderers are to engage a suitably qualified traffic consultant as part of their team and allow for all traffic investigations, surveys and reporting necessary to support the design, approvals and delivery of the project.

The scope, location, duration and methodology of any traffic surveys are to be determined by the traffic consultant based on the project requirements and the needs of the proposed development. This is expected to include investigations necessary to support the design and approval of the Foreshore Road slip lane and associated TfNSW approvals, as well as assessment of parking demand, access arrangements, traffic operations and anticipated car park utilisation.

Tenderers should include within their base scope all traffic investigations, surveys, modelling and reporting reasonably required to complete the design and obtain the necessary approvals.

16) No Quantity Surveyor engagement is required to be included within the Consultant's fee proposal. Council will separately engage a Quantity Surveyor to prepare and manage project cost estimates and Bills of Quantities at the nominated project stages.

The Consultant's role is limited to supporting Council and the Council-appointed Quantity Surveyor by providing coordinated design information, responding to QS enquiries, attending coordination meetings where required, and participating in value management and cost review activities necessary to maintain alignment between the design and project budget.

The Consultant shall provide sufficient design information at each project stage to enable the Council-appointed Quantity Surveyor to prepare concept estimates, detailed design estimates and the IFT Bill of Quantities.

17) The reference to "site management plans for construction" relates to plans, assessments and documentation required to support design development, approvals, environmental assessment and delivery planning for the proposed works.

Council does not require the design consultant to prepare contractor-specific construction management documentation. Accordingly, contractor Safe Work Method Statements (SWMS), Construction Environmental Management Plans (CEMP), Construction Traffic Management Plans (CTMP), site establishment plans, detailed construction methodologies, temporary works documentation and similar contractor delivery documents remain the responsibility of the future construction contractor.

The design consultant is required to identify construction constraints, environmental considerations, staging requirements, traffic management considerations and approval requirements as necessary to inform the design, planning approvals, procurement and project delivery.

18) The Consultant will be required to provide assistance during the construction tender period, including assisting Council with responses to tender RFIs and preparation of addenda where updates to the IFT documentation are required.

The scope does not include review of tender submissions, technical tender evaluations, tender interviews, tender clarifications following tender close, or recommendation of a preferred tenderer.

Tenderers should assume a tender period of approximately four (4) to six (6) weeks and allow for up to ten (10) combined RFI responses and/or addenda during that period.

19) The Consultant shall incorporate Council's review comments, approved tender clarifications, and any addenda issued during the tender period into the final documentation.

Tenderers shall also allow for one review and update of the documentation to IFC following appointment of the successful construction contractor.

This review is intended to address coordination, incorporation of agreed contractor comments, constructability matters, and minor adjustments arising from the successful contractor's review of the documentation.

The scope does not include substantial redesign, re-scoping of the project, or multiple iterations resulting from alternative materials, alternative methodologies, value engineering proposals, or contractor-initiated design changes beyond the single IFC review allowance described above.

20) Any additional investigations that are identified by the Consultant following review of the available information, and which could not have been reasonably identified or quantified at the time of tender, are to be clearly documented in the tender delivery or methodology documentation where possible.

Investigations and services that can be reasonably anticipated as being necessary to complete the design, obtain approvals, or deliver a constructable project are to be included within the Consultant's fixed lump sum fee.

Tenderers should clearly state any assumptions regarding additional investigations in their proposal and nominate any associated provisional allowances where appropriate.
